excerpt: The Frontier Safety Framework is a set of protocols that aims to address severe risks that may arise from powerful capabilities of foundation models.
paraphrase: The Framework is a set of protocols addressing severe risks from powerful foundation model capabilities.

excerpt: It is intended to complement Google’s existing suite of AI responsibility and safety practices, and enable AI innovation and deployment consistent with our AI Principles.
paraphrase: The Framework complements Google's existing AI safety practices and supports innovation consistent with its AI Principles.

excerpt: The Framework is informed by the broader conversation on Frontier AI Safety Frameworks.
paraphrase: The Framework draws on the wider discourse regarding Frontier AI Safety Frameworks.

excerpt: The core components of Frontier AI Safety Frameworks are to:
paraphrase: This introduces the list of core components of Frontier AI Safety Frameworks.

context_stem: The core components of Frontier AI Safety Frameworks are to:
excerpt: Identify capability levels at which AI models without additional mitigations could pose severe risk
paraphrase: One core component is identifying capability levels at which unmitigated models could pose severe risk.

context_stem: The core components of Frontier AI Safety Frameworks are to:
excerpt: Implement protocols to detect the attainment of such capability levels
paraphrase: Another core component is implementing protocols to detect when such capability levels are reached.

context_stem: The core components of Frontier AI Safety Frameworks are to:
excerpt: Prepare and articulate mitigation plans in advance of when such capability levels are attained
paraphrase: Another core component is preparing mitigation plans before such capability levels are reached.

context_stem: The core components of Frontier AI Safety Frameworks are to:
excerpt: Where appropriate, involve external parties to help inform and guide our approach.
paraphrase: Another core component is involving external parties, where appropriate, to inform and guide the approach.

excerpt: In version 2.0 of the Framework, we specify protocols for the detection of capability levels at which models may pose severe risks (which we call “Critical Capability Levels (CCLs)”), and articulate mitigation approaches to address such risks.
paraphrase: Version 2.0 specifies detection protocols for Critical Capability Levels and mitigation approaches for them.

excerpt: At present, the Framework primarily addresses misuse risk, but we also include an exploratory section addressing deceptive alignment risk, focusing on capability levels at which such risks may begin to arise.
paraphrase: The Framework mainly covers misuse risk but also has an exploratory section on deceptive alignment risk.

excerpt: For each type of risk, we define here a set of CCLs and a mitigation approach for them.
paraphrase: For each risk type, the document defines CCLs and a corresponding mitigation approach.

excerpt: Risk assessment will necessarily involve evaluating cross-cutting capabilities such as agency, tool use, reasoning, and scientific understanding.
paraphrase: Risk assessment must evaluate cross-cutting capabilities like agency, tool use, reasoning, and scientific understanding.

excerpt: The safety of frontier AI systems is a global public good.
paraphrase: Frontier AI safety is characterized as a global public good.

excerpt: The protocols here represent our current understanding and recommended approach of how severe frontier AI risks may be anticipated and addressed.
paraphrase: The protocols reflect the current understanding and recommended approach for anticipating and addressing severe frontier AI risks.

excerpt: Importantly, there are certain mitigations whose social value is significantly reduced if not broadly applied to AI systems reaching critical capabilities.
paraphrase: Some mitigations lose much of their social value unless broadly applied across AI systems reaching critical capabilities.

excerpt: These mitigations should be understood as recommendations for the industry collectively: our adoption of them would only result in effective risk mitigation for society if all relevant organizations provide similar levels of protection, and our adoption of the protocols described in this Framework may depend on whether such organizations across the field adopt similar protocols.
paraphrase: The mitigations are framed as industry-wide recommendations, and Google's own adoption may depend on similar adoption by other organizations.

excerpt: The Framework is exploratory and based on early research.
paraphrase: The Framework is described as exploratory and grounded in early research.

excerpt: We may change our approach and recommendations over time as we gain experience and insights on the projected capabilities of future frontier models.
paraphrase: Google may revise its approach and recommendations as it gains more insight into future frontier model capabilities.

excerpt: We will review the Framework periodically and we expect it to evolve substantially as our understanding of the risks and benefits of frontier models improves.
paraphrase: Google commits to periodic review of the Framework and expects it to evolve substantially.

excerpt: See https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/emerging-processes-for-frontier-ai-safety, https://metr.org/blog/2023-09-26-rsp/, https://www.anthropic.com/news/anthropics-responsible-scaling-policy, https://openai.com/preparedness/, https://www.frontiermodelforum.org/updates/issue-brief-components-of-frontier-ai-safety-frameworks/,
paraphrase: A footnote listing external references on frontier AI safety practices.

excerpt: As in, in the context of the Framework, risks of threat actors using critical capabilities of deployed or exfiltrated models to cause harm.
paraphrase: Misuse risk is defined as threat actors using critical capabilities of deployed or exfiltrated models to cause harm.

excerpt: As in, in the context of the Framework, risks of highly autonomous systems purposefully undermining human control over AI systems.
paraphrase: Deceptive alignment risk is defined as highly autonomous systems purposefully undermining human control.

section_heading: 2 - Assessing the Capabilities of Frontier Models
excerpt: delineating when such capability becomes present, and subsequently when the initial mitigation for this capability—automated monitoring—is no longer adequate.
paraphrase: This describes delineating when a capability arises and when automated monitoring, its initial mitigation, ceases to be adequate.

section_heading: 2 - Assessing the Capabilities of Frontier Models
excerpt: We intend to evaluate our most powerful frontier models regularly to check whether their AI capabilities are approaching a CCL.
paraphrase: Google intends to regularly evaluate its most powerful frontier models to check proximity to a CCL.

section_heading: 2 - Assessing the Capabilities of Frontier Models
excerpt: We also intend to evaluate any of these models that could indicate an exceptional increase in capabilities over previous models, and where appropriate, assess the likelihood of such capabilities and risks before and during training.
paraphrase: Google also intends to evaluate models showing exceptional capability increases and, where appropriate, assess risks before and during training.

section_heading: 2 - Assessing the Capabilities of Frontier Models
excerpt: To do so, we will define a set of evaluations called “early warning evaluations,” with a specific “alert threshold” that flags when a CCL may be reached before the evaluations are run again.
paraphrase: Google will define early warning evaluations with alert thresholds flagging approaching CCLs before the next evaluation cycle.

section_heading: 2 - Assessing the Capabilities of Frontier Models
excerpt: In our evaluations, we seek to equip the model with appropriate scaffolding and other augmentations to make it more likely that we are also assessing the capabilities of systems that will likely be produced with the model.
paraphrase: Evaluations aim to equip models with scaffolding and augmentations so downstream system capabilities are also captured.

section_heading: 2 - Assessing the Capabilities of Frontier Models
excerpt: We may run early warning evaluations more frequently or adjust the alert threshold of our evaluations if the rate of progress suggests our safety buffer is no longer adequate.
paraphrase: Google may increase evaluation frequency or adjust alert thresholds if progress suggests the safety buffer is insufficient.

section_heading: 2 - Assessing the Capabilities of Frontier Models
excerpt: Where necessary, early warning evaluations may be supplemented by other evaluations to better understand model capabilities relative to our CCLs.
paraphrase: Additional evaluations may supplement early warning evaluations when needed to clarify capabilities relative to CCLs.

section_heading: 2 - Assessing the Capabilities of Frontier Models
excerpt: We may use additional external evaluators to test a model for relevant capabilities, if evaluators with relevant expertise are needed to provide an additional signal about a model’s proximity to CCLs.
paraphrase: External evaluators may be used to test models when specialized expertise is needed to gauge proximity to CCLs.

excerpt: When a model reaches an alert threshold for a CCL, we will assess the proximity of the model to the CCL and analyze the risk posed, involving internal and external experts as needed.
paraphrase: Upon reaching an alert threshold, Google will assess proximity to the CCL and analyze risk, involving experts as needed.

excerpt: This will inform the formulation and application of a response plan.
paraphrase: The assessment informs the formulation and application of a response plan.

excerpt: Central to most response plans will be the application of the mitigations described later in this document.
paraphrase: Most response plans will center on applying the mitigations described later in the document.

excerpt: For misuse, we have two categories of mitigations: security mitigations intended to prevent the exfiltration of model weights, and deployment mitigations (such as safety fine-tuning and misuse filtering, detection, and response) intended to counter the misuse of critical capabilities in deployments.
paraphrase: Misuse mitigations fall into two categories: security mitigations preventing weight exfiltration, and deployment mitigations countering misuse in deployment.

excerpt: For deceptive alignment risk, automated monitoring may be applied to detect and respond to deceptive behavior for models that meet the first deceptive alignment CCL.
paraphrase: For deceptive alignment risk, automated monitoring may be used for models meeting the first deceptive alignment CCL.

excerpt: Note that these mitigations reflect considerations from the perspective of addressing severe risks from powerful capabilities alone; due to this focused scope, other risk management and security considerations may result in more stringent mitigations applied to a model than specified by the Framework.
paraphrase: The mitigations address only severe capability risks; other considerations may lead to stricter mitigations than the Framework specifies.

excerpt: A model flagged by an alert threshold may be assessed to pose risks for which readily available mitigations (including but not limited to those described below) may not be sufficient.
paraphrase: A flagged model may pose risks that available mitigations cannot sufficiently address.

excerpt: If this happens, the response plan may involve putting deployment or further development on hold until adequate mitigations can be applied.
paraphrase: In such cases, the response plan may pause deployment or development until adequate mitigations exist.

excerpt: Conversely, where model capabilities remain quite distant from a CCL, a response plan may involve the adoption of additional capability assessment processes to flag when heightened mitigations may be required.
paraphrase: If a model remains far from a CCL, the response plan may add capability assessment processes to flag when stronger mitigations are needed.

excerpt: The appropriateness and efficacy of applied mitigations should be reviewed periodically, drawing on information like related misuse or misuse attempt incidents; results from continued post-mitigation testing; statistics about our intelligence, monitoring and escalation processes; and updated threat modeling and risk landscape analysis.
paraphrase: Mitigation appropriateness and efficacy should be periodically reviewed using incident data, post-mitigation testing, monitoring statistics, and updated threat modeling.

excerpt: This section describes our mitigation approach for models that pose risks of severe harm through misuse, and then details our set of misuse CCLs, as well as the mitigations that we provisionally assess as appropriate for them.
paraphrase: This introductory statement outlines that the Misuse section covers mitigation approach, misuse CCLs, and provisional appropriate mitigations.

excerpt: There are two categories of mitigations to address models with misuse critical capabilities: security mitigations intended to prevent the exfiltration of model weights, and deployment mitigations intended to counter the misuse of critical capabilities in deployments.
paraphrase: Misuse mitigations fall into security mitigations against exfiltration and deployment mitigations against misuse in deployment.

excerpt: For security, we have several levels of mitigations, allowing calibration of the robustness of security measures to the risks posed.
paraphrase: Multiple levels of security mitigations allow calibrating robustness to the level of risk.

excerpt: For deployment mitigations, we specify a standard process for applying, assessing, and reviewing mitigations: the aim of this process is to calibrate mitigations to CCLs, and the procedural approach reflects the more iterative and CCL-dependent nature of deployment mitigations.
paraphrase: Deployment mitigations follow a standard process to apply, assess, and review measures calibrated to CCLs, reflecting their iterative nature.

excerpt: Security mitigations against exfiltration risk are important for models reaching CCLs.
paraphrase: Security mitigations against exfiltration are important for models that reach CCLs.

excerpt: This is because the release of model weights may enable the removal of any safeguards trained into or deployed with the model, and hence access (including by threat actors) to any critical capabilities.
paraphrase: Weight release could allow removal of safeguards and give threat actors access to critical capabilities.

excerpt: Here, we rely on the RAND framework to articulate the level of security recommended for each CCL.
paraphrase: The RAND framework is used to articulate recommended security levels for each CCL.

excerpt: When we reference RAND security levels, we are referring to the security principles in their framework, rather than the benchmarks (i.e. concrete measures) also described in the RAND report.
paraphrase: References to RAND security levels denote the framework's security principles, not its concrete benchmark measures.

excerpt: Because AI security is an area of active research, we expect the concrete measures implemented to reach each level of security to evolve substantially.
paraphrase: As AI security is actively evolving research, the concrete measures for each security level are expected to change substantially.

excerpt: The following deployment mitigation process will be applied to models reaching a CCL, allowing for iterative and flexible tailoring of mitigations to each risk and use case.
paraphrase: A deployment mitigation process will be applied to models reaching a CCL, allowing flexible tailoring by risk and use case.

excerpt: Development and assessment of mitigations: safeguards and an accompanying safety case are developed by iterating on the following:
paraphrase: Step one is developing and assessing mitigations, with safeguards and a safety case built through iteration.

context_stem: Development and assessment of mitigations: safeguards and an accompanying safety case are developed by iterating on the following:
excerpt: Developing and improving a suite of safeguards targeting the capability. This includes, as appropriate, safety fine-tuning, misuse filtering and detection, and response protocols.
paraphrase: Sub-step: developing and improving safeguards targeting the capability, including fine-tuning, filtering, detection, and response protocols as appropriate.

context_stem: Development and assessment of mitigations: safeguards and an accompanying safety case are developed by iterating on the following:
excerpt: Assessing the robustness of these mitigations against the risk posed through assurance evaluations and threat modeling research. The assessment takes the form of a safety case, taking into account factors such as the likelihood and consequences of misuse.
paraphrase: Sub-step: assessing mitigation robustness via assurance evaluations and threat modeling, producing a safety case considering likelihood and consequences of misuse.

excerpt: Pre-deployment review of safety case: general availability deployment of a model takes place only after the appropriate corporate governance body determines the safety case regarding each CCL the model has reached to be adequate.
paraphrase: Step two: general availability deployment occurs only after a corporate governance body deems the safety case for each reached CCL adequate.

excerpt: Post-deployment review of safety case: the safety case will be updated through red-teaming and revisions to our threat models.
paraphrase: Step three: the safety case is updated post-deployment via red-teaming and revised threat models.

excerpt: The safeguards for the model may be updated as well to ensure continued adequacy.
paraphrase: Model safeguards may also be updated to maintain continued adequacy.

excerpt: The table below details a set of CCLs we have identified through ongoing analysis of the CBRN, Cyber, and Machine Learning R&D risk domains.
paraphrase: The table describes CCLs identified from analysis of CBRN, Cyber, and Machine Learning R&D risk domains.

excerpt: We expect these to evolve over time.
paraphrase: The CCLs are expected to evolve over time.

excerpt: We recommend a security level to each of these CCLs, which reflect our assessment of the minimum appropriate level of security the field of frontier AI should apply to models reaching each CCL.
paraphrase: Each CCL is assigned a recommended security level reflecting the minimum appropriate security the frontier AI field should apply.

excerpt: In practice, our overall security posture may commonly exceed the baseline levels recommended here.
paraphrase: Actual security posture may often exceed the recommended baseline levels.

excerpt: These recommended security levels reflect our current thinking and may be adjusted if our empirical understanding of the risks changes.
paraphrase: Recommended security levels reflect current thinking and may be adjusted as empirical understanding evolves.

excerpt: This may occur if, for example, a model does not possess capabilities meaningfully different from other widely available models that have not demonstrably caused or contributed to severe risks, or if we assess that the benefits of the open release of model weights outweigh the risks.
paraphrase: Adjustment might occur if a model's capabilities aren't meaningfully different from other benign widely-available models, or if open release benefits are judged to outweigh risks.

excerpt: Relatedly, we believe these recommendations will only be effective if the entire frontier AI field applies them, and of limited social utility if not.
paraphrase: The recommendations are believed effective only if adopted across the entire frontier AI field.

paraphrase: Most advanced risk formerly captured by this CCL is now covered under the misalignment section.

excerpt: For example, through the use of a self-replicating CBRN agent. Compared to a counterfactual of not using generative AI systems.
paraphrase: Example given: a self-replicating CBRN agent, compared against a counterfactual of no generative AI use.

excerpt: E.g. deletion or exfiltration of critical information, or destroying or disabling key systems.
paraphrase: Examples of end-to-end cyberattacks include deleting/exfiltrating critical information or disabling key systems.

excerpt: E.g. deletion or exfiltration of sensitive information/disruption of key systems of organizations with strong security posture, or the creation of predictable and large-scale effects on critical national infrastructure.
paraphrase: Examples of high impact cyber attacks include disruption of strongly secured organizations or large-scale effects on critical infrastructure.

excerpt: Relative to the counterfactual of using 2024 AI technology and tooling.
paraphrase: The order-of-magnitude comparison is relative to 2024 AI technology and tooling.

excerpt: This section describes an initial approach for addressing risks of deceptive alignment.
paraphrase: This section presents an initial approach to addressing deceptive alignment risks.

excerpt: By "deceptive alignment," we mean the risk that AI systems purposefully undermine human control over AI systems.
paraphrase: Deceptive alignment is defined as AI systems purposefully undermining human control.

excerpt: While we do not express any opinion here about how likely it is for deceptive alignment to arise, this section’s provisions aim to prepare for this possibility.
paraphrase: No view is expressed on the likelihood of deceptive alignment, but the section aims to prepare for the possibility.

excerpt: Note that the effective mitigation of deceptive alignment risk requires the application of safeguards to all AI systems reaching critical capabilities.
paraphrase: Effective mitigation of deceptive alignment risk requires safeguards across all AI systems reaching critical capabilities.

excerpt: It is important that the industry adopts strategies for addressing this risk: what is detailed in this section represents one possible approach for doing so.
paraphrase: Industry-wide adoption of strategies is important; this section presents one possible approach.

section_heading: Mitigation Approach and Critical Capability Levels
excerpt: An initial mitigation approach focuses on detecting when models might develop a baseline instrumental reasoning ability at which they have the potential to undermine human control, assuming no additional mitigations were applied.
paraphrase: The initial approach focuses on detecting a baseline instrumental reasoning ability that could enable undermining human control absent mitigations.

section_heading: Mitigation Approach and Critical Capability Levels
excerpt: When models reach this capability level, we believe applying an automated monitor to the model’s explicit reasoning (e.g. chain-of-thought output) is an effective mitigation.
paraphrase: At this capability level, automated monitoring of explicit reasoning output is believed to be an effective mitigation.

section_heading: Mitigation Approach and Critical Capability Levels
excerpt: Once a model is capable of effective instrumental reasoning in ways that cannot be monitored, additional mitigations may be warranted—the development of which is an area of active research.
paraphrase: Once instrumental reasoning becomes unmonitorable, additional mitigations, still under active research, may be needed.

excerpt: Instrumental Reasoning Level 1: the instrumental reasoning abilities of the model enable enough situational awareness (ability to work out and use relevant details of its deployment setting) and stealth (ability to circumvent basic oversight mechanisms) such that, absent additional mitigations, we cannot rule out the model significantly undermining human control.
paraphrase: Instrumental Reasoning Level 1 is defined by sufficient situational awareness and stealth that, without mitigations, the model might significantly undermine human control.

section_heading: Table 2: Deceptive Alignment CCLs and Mitigations
context_stem: Row: Instrumental Reasoning Level 1. Column: Mitigation
excerpt: Automated monitoring: a monitoring system to detect illicit use of instrumental reasoning capabilities in a model’s chain-of-thought and use it in high-stakes deployments where there is significant risk of the model undermining human control.
paraphrase: Mitigation is automated monitoring of chain-of-thought to detect illicit instrumental reasoning use in high-stakes deployments.

section_heading: Table 2: Deceptive Alignment CCLs and Mitigations
locator: Table 2 / Instrumental Reasoning Level 2 / Deceptive Alignment CCL
context_stem: Row: Instrumental Reasoning Level 2. Column: Deceptive Alignment CCL
excerpt: Instrumental Reasoning Level 2: the instrumental reasoning abilities of the model enable enough situational awareness and stealth that, even when relevant model outputs (including, e.g., scratchpads) are being monitored, we cannot detect or rule out the risk of a model significantly undermining human control.
paraphrase: Instrumental Reasoning Level 2 is defined by capability sufficient that even monitored outputs cannot detect or rule out significant undermining of human control.

section_heading: Table 2: Deceptive Alignment CCLs and Mitigations
context_stem: Row: Instrumental Reasoning Level 2. Column: Mitigation
excerpt: Future work: We are actively researching approaches to addressing models that reach this CCL.
paraphrase: For this CCL, mitigation approaches are still under active research.

excerpt: Looking forward, we expect the approach to deceptive alignment risks to take a similar form as the deployment mitigation process.
paraphrase: The deceptive alignment approach is expected to resemble the deployment mitigation process.

excerpt: For each deceptive alignment risk, AI developers should:
paraphrase: This introduces recommended actions for AI developers for each deceptive alignment risk.

context_stem: For each deceptive alignment risk, AI developers should:
excerpt: Develop a safety case based on the model’s capabilities and the mitigations applied and tested.
paraphrase: Developers should build a safety case based on model capabilities and tested mitigations.

context_stem: Develop a safety case based on the model’s capabilities and the mitigations applied and tested.
excerpt: Such safety cases would make the case that the likelihood of deceptive alignment risk would be low enough for safe deployment, even if the model were trying to meaningfully undermine human control.
paraphrase: The safety case would argue the risk of deceptive alignment is low enough for safe deployment even under adversarial assumptions.

context_stem: For each deceptive alignment risk, AI developers should:
excerpt: Test the mitigations applied to models via red-teaming protocols called “control evaluations,” to determine whether they meet the requirements of the safety case.
paraphrase: Developers should test mitigations via control evaluations to see if they meet the safety case's requirements.

excerpt: The approach above relies on two safety cases centering respectively on the claims that:
paraphrase: The approach depends on two distinct safety case claims.

context_stem: The approach above relies on two safety cases centering respectively on the claims that:
excerpt: A model does not meet a threshold CCL and therefore would be incapable of substantially undermining human control.
paraphrase: Claim one: the model does not meet a threshold CCL and thus cannot substantially undermine human control.

context_stem: The approach above relies on two safety cases centering respectively on the claims that:
excerpt: An automated monitoring process that is validated by a control evaluation is adequate for catching the model’s malicious behavior.
paraphrase: Claim two: a control-evaluation-validated automated monitoring process is adequate to catch malicious behavior.

excerpt: Once neither of these apply, that is, once automated monitoring is no longer adequate/can no longer pass a control evaluation, a model is deemed to have reached the second CCL.
paraphrase: When neither safety case applies (monitoring no longer adequate or fails control evaluation), the model is deemed to have reached the second CCL.

excerpt: For Google models, when alert thresholds are reached, the response plan will be reviewed and approved by appropriate corporate governance bodies such as the Google DeepMind AGI Safety Council, Google DeepMind Responsibility and Safety Council, and/or Google Trust & Compliance Council.
paraphrase: Upon alert threshold triggers, the response plan is reviewed and approved by named corporate governance bodies.

excerpt: The Google DeepMind AGI Safety Council will periodically review the implementation of the Framework.
paraphrase: The AGI Safety Council will periodically review Framework implementation.

excerpt: If we assess that a model has reached a CCL that poses an unmitigated and material risk to overall public safety, we aim to share information with appropriate government authorities where it will facilitate the development of safe AI.
paraphrase: If a CCL poses unmitigated material risk to public safety, Google aims to share information with relevant government authorities.

excerpt: Where appropriate, and subject to adequate confidentiality and security measures and considerations around proprietary and sensitive information, this information may include:
paraphrase: This introduces categories of information that may be disclosed, subject to confidentiality safeguards.

context_stem: Where appropriate, and subject to adequate confidentiality and security measures and considerations around proprietary and sensitive information, this information may include:
excerpt: Model information: characteristics of the AI model relevant to the risk it may pose with its critical capabilities.
paraphrase: One disclosable category is model information relevant to the risk posed by its critical capabilities.

context_stem: Where appropriate, and subject to adequate confidentiality and security measures and considerations around proprietary and sensitive information, this information may include:
excerpt: Evaluation results: such as details about the evaluation design, the results, and any robustness tests.
paraphrase: Another disclosable category is evaluation results, including design, results, and robustness tests.

context_stem: Where appropriate, and subject to adequate confidentiality and security measures and considerations around proprietary and sensitive information, this information may include:
excerpt: Mitigation plans: descriptions of our mitigation plans and how they are expected to reduce the risk.
paraphrase: Another disclosable category is mitigation plans and their expected risk reduction.

excerpt: We may also consider disclosing information to other external organizations to promote shared learning and coordinated risk mitigation.
paraphrase: Disclosure to other external organizations may also be considered to promote shared learning and coordinated mitigation.

excerpt: We will continue to review and evolve our disclosure process over time.
paraphrase: The disclosure process will continue to be reviewed and evolved.

excerpt: We expect the Framework to evolve substantially as our understanding of the risks and benefits of frontier models improves, and we will publish substantive revisions as appropriate.
paraphrase: The Framework is expected to evolve substantially, with substantive revisions published as appropriate.

excerpt: Issues that we aim to address in future versions of the Framework include:
paraphrase: This introduces a list of issues planned for future Framework versions.

context_stem: Issues that we aim to address in future versions of the Framework include:
excerpt: Greater precision in risk modeling: While we have updated our CCLs and underlying threat models from version 1.0, there remains significant room for improvement in understanding the risks posed by models in different domains, and refining our set of CCLs.
paraphrase: Future work includes greater precision in risk modeling, despite updates since version 1.0, as room remains for improved understanding and CCL refinement.

context_stem: Issues that we aim to address in future versions of the Framework include:
excerpt: Capability elicitation: Our evaluators continue to improve their ability to estimate what capabilities may be attainable by different threat actors with access to our models, taking into account a growing number of possible post-training enhancements.
paraphrase: Future work includes improving estimation of attainable capabilities by threat actors, accounting for post-training enhancements.

context_stem: Issues that we aim to address in future versions of the Framework include:
excerpt: Updated set of risks and mitigations: There may be additional risk domains and critical capabilities that fall into scope as AI capabilities improve and the external environment changes.
paraphrase: Future work may address additional risk domains and critical capabilities as AI capabilities and the external environment evolve.

context_stem: Updated set of risks and mitigations: There may be additional risk domains and critical capabilities that fall into scope as AI capabilities improve and the external environment changes.
excerpt: Future work will aim to include additional pressing risks, which may include additional risk domains or higher CCLs within existing domains.
paraphrase: Future work aims to add pressing risks, possibly new domains or higher CCLs within existing domains.

context_stem: Issues that we aim to address in future versions of the Framework include:
excerpt: Deceptive alignment approach beyond automated monitoring: We are actively researching approaches to addressing models that reach the “Instrumental Reasoning Level 2” CCL.
paraphrase: Future work includes deceptive alignment approaches beyond automated monitoring, actively researched for the Instrumental Reasoning Level 2 CCL.

context_stem: Issues that we aim to address in future versions of the Framework include:
excerpt: Broader approach to ML R&D risks: The risks posed by models reaching our ML R&D CCLs may require measures beyond security and deployment mitigations, to ensure that safety measures and social institutions continue to be able to adapt to new AI capabilities amidst possible acceleration in AI development.
paraphrase: ML R&D CCL risks may require measures beyond security and deployment mitigations to keep safety measures and institutions adaptive amid accelerating AI development.

context_stem: Broader approach to ML R&D risks
excerpt: We are actively researching appropriate responses to these scenarios.
paraphrase: Appropriate responses to these ML R&D risk scenarios are being actively researched.
